newsitem.title: USA: Massachusett's electricity deregulation model out.
newsitem.headline: Massachusett's electricity deregulation model out.

text.p: The Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities (DPU) Monday presented its model rules and legislative proposal for a restructured electric utility industry.
The restructuring plan promises to reduce costs for all electric consumers when it goes into effect Jan. 1, 1998, the DPU said in a statement.

Recent agreements reached between the state's attorney general's office and Boston Edison, Eastern Utilities Associates and Massachusetts Electric, a subsidiary of New England System will come under the proposal.
The MassElectric agreement "is our number one priority," said DPU chairman John Howe.
The restructuring plan "is consistent, we believe, with what we have seen of the agreements," Howe said.

While MassElectric has submitted a formal plan to divest itself of its generating assets, the other utilities have not. The Eastern Utilities plan is "an MOU (Memorandum of Understanding)" Howe said, adding the Boston Edison agreement was not that fully developed.
The proposal includes: -- a framework to ensure full and fair competition in the generation of electric power and model rules to implement this framework.
-- a commitment to ensure the continued safety and reliability of the industry.

-- transition measures to facilitate the change from the regulated monopoly framework to a competitive market, such as recovery of so-called stranded costs, assistance to municipalities regarding property taxes on power plants and rate unbundling.

-- a description of the positions the DPU will take on issues subject to federal jurisdiction, and a legislative proposal for consideration by the Massachusetts Legislature that supports the new framework and provides the DPU with the authority needed to fully implement the plan.

-- a commitment that the restructured electric industry continue to deliver certain public policy benefits provided by electric companies relating to the environment, consumer protection and electric rate discounts for low-income consumers equivalent to those currently in place.

In February 1995, the DPU began its comprehensive inquiry into how all consumers of electricity in Massachusetts could benefit from the realities of a changing and increasingly competitive power generation market. Since then, the DPU has received comments from more than 200 participants with an interest in the outcome of this investigation.
